Kimberly Davis-Stepney

Welcome to my Professional Portfolio. This portfolio represents my journey through the Master of Arts in Teaching program with a concentration in Family and Consumer Sciences at Valdosta State University. Throughout this program, I have developed knowledge, skills, and professional dispositions necessary to become an effective educator. This website highlights my coursework, teaching philosophy, professional growth, and educational experiences. It serves as a reflection of my commitment to lifelong learning and my passion for preparing students with practical life skills that support success in school, careers, and everyday life.

Recipe for an Educator
SERVES: A full classroom · PREP TIME: One master's degree

Ingredients

  • 1 heaping cup of high expectations
  • 2 tbsp encouragement, packed
  • A generous pinch of structure and grace
  • Real-world experience, folded in gently
  • Curiosity about emerging technology, to taste

Method

Combine high expectations with encouragement until a learning environment forms where students feel respected, challenged, and empowered to reach their full potential. Fold in real-world experience so academic and life skills develop side by side.

Yield: Confident, career-ready students — and one lifelong learner who keeps growing alongside them.
01 · About

About Me

Hello, and welcome to my portfolio! My name is Kimberly Davis-Stepney, and I am a passionate educator dedicated to preparing students for success both in and beyond the classroom. I currently teach Culinary Arts in a College and Career Academy, where I have the opportunity to help students develop technical skills, workplace readiness, confidence, and a lifelong appreciation for learning.

My educational journey has been driven by a commitment to continuous growth and service. I earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Paralegal Studies and am currently completing my Master of Arts in Teaching with a concentration in Family and Consumer Sciences. Through my graduate studies, I have expanded my knowledge of instructional strategies, classroom management, technology integration, assessment practices, and student-centered learning. These experiences have strengthened my belief that every student can succeed when provided with meaningful opportunities, clear expectations, and supportive relationships.

As an educator, I believe that structure and grace go hand in hand. I strive to create a learning environment where students feel respected, challenged, and empowered to reach their full potential. My teaching philosophy combines high expectations with encouragement, helping students develop both academic and life skills that will serve them well in their future careers and personal lives.

Outside of the classroom, I enjoy spending time with my family, exploring new recipes, and finding creative ways to connect real-world experiences to learning. I am passionate about culinary arts, career and technical education, and helping students discover their strengths and interests. I also enjoy learning about emerging technologies and exploring how they can be used responsibly and effectively in education.

This portfolio represents my growth throughout the Master of Arts in Teaching program and highlights the knowledge, skills, and experiences that have shaped me as an educator. I am proud of the work showcased here and look forward to continuing my journey as a lifelong learner and Family and Consumer Sciences professional.

02 · Reflection

Critical Philosophy of Education

Education is more than a transmission of knowledge; it is the foundation for developing informed, responsible, and compassionate young people who are prepared to contribute to society. As a Family and Consumer Sciences teacher specializing in Culinary Arts, I believe schools should provide students with both academic knowledge and the practical life skills necessary to succeed in college, careers, and their communities. My philosophy of education is grounded primarily in essentialism, incorporating elements of constructivism and social reconstructionism. Together, these orientations shape my beliefs about the purpose of education, the role of the teacher, and the responsibility of schools to prepare students for lifelong learning.

Essentialism serves as the foundation of my educational philosophy because it emphasizes mastery of core knowledge, high expectations, discipline, and personal responsibility. William C. Bagley (1938) argued that schools should provide students with the essential knowledge and skills necessary for productive citizenship and lifelong success, and that systematic, sequenced instruction under a knowledgeable teacher — not incidental or unguided discovery — is what builds genuine competence. As a culinary arts instructor, I believe students must first master foundational concepts such as food safety, sanitation, knife skills, culinary terminology, and professional kitchen procedures before advancing to more complex techniques. Establishing clear expectations, consistent routines, and accountability — principles central to Bagley's (1938) platform — creates a structured learning environment where students can develop confidence, competence, and professionalism.

While I value a structured learning environment, I also believe students learn best through active participation and meaningful experiences. This belief aligns with constructivism and the work of John Dewey (1938), who argued that education should be rooted in experience and problem-solving, and that not all experience is automatically educative; experience should be organized and connected to prior learning to produce real growth. Culinary education naturally provides opportunities for experiential learning as students apply mathematical reasoning through recipe conversions, scientific principles through food chemistry, literacy skills through recipe interpretation, and collaboration through kitchen laboratory experiences. Rather than simply memorizing information, students develop deeper understanding by applying concepts in authentic situations that mirror the expectations of the culinary industry — a constructivist emphasis that Dewey (1938) placed at the center of meaningful schooling.

My philosophy is also influenced by social reconstructionism, which frames education as a means of improving society and preparing students to become engaged citizens. George Counts (1932) challenged teachers to use schools as a deliberate force for shaping a more just social order rather than simply transmitting the existing one, insisting that educators could not evade responsibility for the kind of society their students would go on to build. Food is deeply connected to culture, community, and human relationships. In my classroom, students explore diverse cuisines, examine cultural traditions, and develop an appreciation for perspectives different from their own. Through service-learning opportunities, career exploration, and community partnerships, students learn that culinary skills extend beyond the kitchen and can positively impact individuals and communities, consistent with Counts's (1932) vision of schooling as a force for social improvement. I believe education should empower students to think critically, solve problems ethically, and contribute meaningfully to the world around them.

These philosophical beliefs directly influence my instructional practices. I view my role as both educator and mentor who creates a safe, respectful, and inclusive classroom environment where students have the opportunity to succeed. I believe students thrive when expectations are clear, instruction is engaging, and mistakes are treated as opportunities for growth rather than failure — an approach that draws on Bagley's (1938) insistence on discipline and Dewey's (1938) insistence on learning through experience in equal measure. Building trusting relationships with students, families, colleagues, and community partners creates a supportive learning environment that encourages confidence, resilience, and personal responsibility.

Technology also plays an important role in my philosophy of education. I intentionally integrate digital tools to enhance instruction, differentiate learning, and promote collaboration. These resources provide multiple pathways for students to access content, demonstrate understanding, and develop digital literacy skills essential for success in today's workforce. However, technology should complement, not replace, the authentic hands-on learning experiences that are central to culinary arts education.

Ultimately, I believe the purpose of education is to prepare students not only for employment but also for lifelong learning and responsible citizenship. Success is measured by more than academic achievement; it is reflected in students' ability to think critically, communicate effectively, collaborate with others, and adapt to new challenges. My goal is to inspire students to become confident, ethical, and resilient individuals who continue learning long after they leave my classroom. Every lesson I teach is an opportunity to develop both technical competence and strong character, empowering students to build meaningful futures while making positive contributions to their communities.

References

Bagley, W. C. (1938). An essentialist's platform for the advancement of American education. Educational Administration and Supervision, 24(4), 241–256.

Counts, G. S. (1932). Dare the school build a new social order? John Day Company.

Dewey, J. (1938). Experience and education. Macmillan.

03 · Practice

My Classroom

Classroom Layout, Design, and Flow

My Culinary Arts classroom is designed to support flexibility, collaboration, creativity, and student choice. Group tables allow students to work together when planning menus, evaluating recipes, solving culinary problems, or completing team projects. The tables can also be separated when students need independent learning space. A small-group station provides an area for conferences, peer support, and differentiated instruction, while the bar-height table offers students the option to sit or stand while working. The calming corner gives students a quiet place to regroup when they feel overwhelmed.

The demonstration station includes a camera connected to the smartboard so every student can clearly observe cooking techniques, food preparation procedures, and safety practices. After demonstrations, students can work in teams to test recipes, assign kitchen roles, record results, and discuss possible improvements. Independent activities may include recipe research, cost calculations, reflections, or assessments. Classroom rules, organized supplies, bookshelves, a student bulletin board, and designated phone storage help maintain structure and encourage responsibility. Overall, the classroom reflects my belief that structure and grace go hand in hand. Students are provided with clear expectations while also having opportunities to communicate, create community, learn from mistakes, and take ownership of their growth as culinary students.

04 · Program Reflection

Discovering Your FRAME

Our FRAME is made up of the values we hold, our culture and background, and the life experiences — chosen and unchosen — that shape how we see the world. For this program assignment, I built a photo collage of my family, roots, education, and the places I've called home, paired with a reflective essay.

Discovering My FRAME · Kimberly Davis-Stepney · Valdosta State University

Everyone views the world through a frame built from three things: the values we hold, the culture and background we come from, and the experiences that have shaped our lives, both chosen and unchosen. When I sat down to think about my own frame, I realized it could not be captured in a single image. It had to be told in layers: my family, my roots, my education, and the many places I have called home. Each of these pieces has shaped how I see the world, how I show up as a teacher, and how I show up as a mother and a wife.

Family

At the center of my frame is my family. I am a mother to three daughters and one son, and I am also a bonus mom to a daughter from a previous relationship, which has taught me that family is not only defined by biology but by love and commitment. My husband is active-duty Army, and that single fact has quietly organized almost every other part of my frame. My oldest two daughters are now grown; one just graduated high school and will join her older sister this fall at Georgia Southern University, where she is majoring in Nursing. My youngest daughter and son are still in elementary school, keeping me on my toes in an entirely different way. Raising children across such a wide age range, while moving frequently as a military family, has made me both flexible and fiercely protective of the stability we do manage to create. My family is not just a photo on a slide; it is the reason behind every decision I have made, from the schools I picked to the career paths I pursued.

Roots: Gloucester, Virginia

Before I was a teacher, a mother, or a military spouse, I was a girl growing up in Gloucester, Virginia. Gloucester is a place most people have never heard of, but it carries real history. It is the birthplace of Walter Reed, the physician who helped confirm that yellow fever was spread by mosquitoes, a discovery that changed public health forever. Gloucester is also home to Rosewell, a plantation whose ruins still stand today, fabled for a staircase once said to be wide enough to ride a horse down. I grew up visiting these places as a child, and they gave me an early sense that history is not something that only lives in textbooks; it lives in the ground we walk on. I graduated from Gloucester High School, and that small-town foundation gave me the grounding I would carry into every new city and country I later lived in.

Education

My educational path has not been a straight line, and I have come to see that as one of the more honest parts of my frame. I began college at Chowan University, majoring in Criminal Justice. Wanting to be closer to home, I transferred to Norfolk State University, but life pulled me in a different direction, and I stepped away from school for a season to build a career in cosmetology instead. That was not a detour I regret; it taught me a trade, patience, and how to work directly with people, skills that still show up in my classroom today. Eventually I returned to finish my undergraduate degree at Liberty University, this time earning a Bachelor of Science in Paralegal Studies. After moving to Georgia and taking a job as a substitute teacher, I found myself drawn to the classroom in a way I had not expected. When I landed a position teaching Culinary Arts, I decided I wanted to be fully invested in that role, not just present for it, so I enrolled in a Master of Arts in Teaching program in Family and Consumer Sciences. That decision reflects something core to my frame: I would rather go back and earn the credentials to do something well than coast on what I already have. Today, along with my paralegal degree, I hold a cosmetology license in both Virginia and Texas and a Pharmacy Technician certification, evidence of a habit I have built over the years of following opportunity wherever it leads and preparing myself properly when I get there.

Places I've Lived, Then and Now

The last piece of my frame is geography. It started at Fort Eustis, Virginia, where I met my husband, an active-duty soldier, and we were married. From there, the Army sent us to Baumholder, Germany, where we lived for three years. I fell in love with the culture, the food, and the people there, and I came home with a wider sense of the world than I had left with. Next came Fort Hood, Texas, for five years, where I gave birth to my two youngest children and went back to work as a manager for a salon franchise. From Texas we moved to Pittsford, New York, a small, beautiful village outside Rochester that sits along the Erie Canal, quiet and unlike anywhere I had lived before. For the last four years, we have been at Fort Stewart, Georgia, which is where I built my teaching career and where my children have grown up the most. This October our family has orders to move again, this time to Fort Riley, Kansas. I will be honest: I am not excited about this move, and I am still working through the shock of it. For now it just feels like the next stop the Army has chosen for us, and I am giving myself room to process that instead of pretending the excitement is there when it is not.

Conclusion

Taken together, my family, my roots, my winding education, and the string of places I have lived make up my frame. They explain why I value stability even while living a life that rarely offers it, why I believe in finishing what I start even when the path bends, and why I can walk into a new classroom, a new state, and know that I have done this before. My frame is still being built.

Technology Integration

Teacher Use of Technology to Customize Instruction

As a Culinary Arts instructor, I use TeachShare and Google Slides to design and deliver standards-based instruction that meets the diverse needs of my students. TeachShare provides access to instructional resources, lesson plans, and activities that align with Georgia CTAE standards. These resources allow me to adapt lessons, incorporate best practices, and provide engaging learning experiences for students with varying readiness levels.

I use Google Slides to create visually engaging presentations that include photographs, diagrams, vocabulary, step-by-step cooking procedures, and embedded instructional videos. Students benefit from having access to these presentations through Canvas, allowing them to review concepts before, during, and after laboratory activities. This approach supports visual learners, English language learners, and students who need additional time or repeated instruction while also providing enrichment opportunities for advanced learners.

Student Use of Technology to Enhance Learning

Students use technology to demonstrate their understanding, collaborate with classmates, and create authentic culinary products. Throughout the course, students use Canva to design professional-quality menus, recipe cards, nutrition infographics, food safety posters, and career exploration projects that strengthen both their culinary knowledge and digital design skills. Students also use Google Slides to develop presentations that explain cooking techniques, kitchen safety procedures, culinary careers, and laboratory reflections. These presentations encourage students to communicate their learning while incorporating images, research, and multimedia elements.

To stay organized during culinary laboratories and long-term projects, students use Google Keep to create digital checklists, record recipe notes, manage assignments, and track project deadlines. This tool promotes organization, responsibility, and independent learning while helping students develop workplace skills that transfer beyond the classroom.

Integrating technology into my Culinary Arts classroom has transformed the way students learn and demonstrate their understanding. Digital tools provide opportunities for collaboration, creativity, differentiation, and authentic assessment while supporting hands-on laboratory experiences. By combining industry-recognized resources with engaging instructional technology, I help students develop the technical, digital, and employability skills necessary for success in college, careers, and lifelong learning.

07 · Growth

Looking Back

When I entered the MAT program, my first goal was simply to finish. I also wanted to invest in myself and become the best teacher possible for my students. At the time, I sometimes felt like an imposter who was “faking it until I made it.” Although I had content knowledge and practical experience, I wanted the confidence, preparation, and professional skills needed to become a more effective educator.

My original goals have not changed, but they have grown. As I complete the program, I recognize how much I have developed as a teacher. I have gained valuable skills in lesson planning, assessment, classroom management, technology integration, and meeting diverse student needs. These experiences have helped me become more intentional in my teaching and more confident in the decisions I make each day.

My immediate goal is to return to the classroom this year fully focused on implementing the strategies and skills I learned throughout the MAT program. I have not decided what my next educational step will be. I may pursue an Ed.S. degree or return to school for a Juris Master since law has always been a passion of mine. I would also be interested in becoming involved in educational law in some capacity. No matter which path I choose, completing this program has shown me that investing in my education strengthens both my future and the learning experiences I provide for my students.

08 · Integration

Synthesis

My experience in the Master of Arts in Teaching program helped me connect my knowledge of Culinary Arts with the principles of effective teaching. Entering the program as an employed teacher allowed me to immediately apply what I learned in my own classroom. Each course encouraged me to examine my teaching decisions, reflect on student needs, and develop a stronger understanding of how students learn. The program gave me opportunities to study educational theory while testing practical strategies in both classroom and lab settings. As a result, I have become a more intentional, reflective, and student-centered educator.

Before beginning the program, I often planned lessons by considering what content needed to be covered and what activity students would complete. I now begin with the standard, identify the learning objective, and determine what evidence will show that students have learned the material. From there, I select instructional strategies, assessments, and supports that fit the needs of my students. This process has helped me understand that an engaging activity is not automatically an effective lesson. Each activity, demonstration, and lab should have a clear purpose connected to student learning.

The individual courses also expanded my understanding of my responsibilities as a teacher. I learned that my role includes more than delivering content. I am responsible for creating a safe and inclusive learning environment, communicating effectively, supporting literacy, using assessment data, and providing students with different ways to learn. I also have a responsibility to model professionalism, ethical technology use, and respect for others. These courses helped me see how planning, instruction, assessment, communication, and classroom management work together. When one of these areas is weak, it can affect the entire learning experience.

One of the courses that had the greatest impact on me was Classroom Management. This course helped me develop my belief that structure and grace go hand in hand. Culinary Arts requires strong classroom management because students work with knives, heat, equipment, and food while moving around the kitchen. I learned that effective management begins before a problem occurs through clear expectations, consistent routines, and well-taught procedures. I also learned to use relationship-based strategies and logical consequences instead of viewing discipline as punishment alone. Applying these strategies has made managing large groups in the classroom and culinary lab more manageable. I now feel more confident holding students accountable while still giving them opportunities to learn from mistakes and make better choices.

Another course that significantly influenced my practice was Planning, Assessment, and Differentiation. This course changed how I design lessons and measure student learning. I learned to align standards, objectives, activities, and assessments rather than treating them as separate parts of a lesson plan. I also gained a better understanding of Bloom’s Taxonomy and the difference between simply recalling information and applying knowledge in an authentic setting. In Culinary Arts, students may first identify a cooking method, but they should eventually be able to select the appropriate method, perform the technique safely, and explain the results. The course also encouraged me to plan for students with different readiness levels, strengths, and learning needs. I now provide clearer directions, model processes, divide complex tasks into manageable steps, and allow students multiple ways to demonstrate understanding.

Other courses strengthened these changes. Content Area Literacy helped me recognize that reading recipes, understanding industry vocabulary, and explaining culinary procedures are meaningful forms of literacy. Classroom Technology Integration taught me to select technology according to the learning goal instead of using it simply because it is available. My internship experiences allowed me to apply these ideas in my own classroom while receiving feedback from my mentor teacher and university supervisor. That feedback helped me reflect more honestly on my pacing, student engagement, directions, and instructional decisions.

As I complete the MAT program, I no longer feel that I am only trying to make it through each day. I have a stronger professional foundation and a clearer understanding of why I make certain instructional choices. I know that becoming the best teacher for my students is an ongoing process, but I now have the knowledge and confidence to continue growing. My next goal is to return to the classroom fully focused on implementing the strategies I learned throughout the program. Most importantly, the MAT program helped me move from feeling like an imposter to recognizing myself as a prepared, reflective, and capable educator.

09 · Next Steps

Looking Forward — Professional Learning Plan

Specific Strengths

One of my strengths is creating meaningful, hands-on learning experiences. My courses allow students to connect academic knowledge with practical skills they can use in the workplace and their daily lives. I design lessons that combine direct instruction, demonstrations, collaboration, and labs. During lab activities, students practice technical skills while also developing communication, time management, problem-solving, and teamwork. These authentic experiences help students understand the purpose behind what they are learning.

Another strength is building supportive relationships while maintaining structure. My classroom management philosophy is that structure and grace go hand in hand. I establish clear expectations for respect, responsibility, safety, and effort while recognizing that students have different needs and circumstances. The strategies I have learned throughout the MAT program have strengthened my ability to manage larger groups, communicate expectations, and respond to student behavior consistently. I have also become more confident in creating a classroom environment where students feel respected and encouraged to improve.

Special Areas of Challenge

An area of challenge I find is differentiating instruction in a large Culinary Arts classroom. Students enter the program with different reading levels, learning needs, technical abilities, and levels of confidence. Some students understand a demonstration quickly, while others need written directions, visual examples, repeated modeling, or additional practice. Providing these supports while supervising an active culinary lab can be difficult.

The next challenge is using assessment data consistently to guide instruction. Culinary Arts requires students to demonstrate both academic knowledge and hands-on performance. Written tests do not always show what students can accomplish in the lab, while successful completion of a recipe may not reveal whether they understand the principles behind each technique. I want to improve how I collect and analyze different forms of assessment data so I can provide targeted feedback and adjust instruction.

Professional Growth Goals

Goal 1: Differentiate instruction to meet diverse student needs.
By July 2027, I will design and implement differentiated supports in at least two lessons or laboratory experiences per instructional unit. These supports may include visual directions, vocabulary assistance, step-by-step task cards, flexible grouping, modified assignments, or additional demonstrations. I will review student work and assessment results to determine which supports are most effective.

Goal 2: Improve assessment and data-informed instruction.
By July 2027, I will develop and consistently use a balanced assessment system that includes formative checks, written assessments, performance-based lab rubrics, and student self-assessments. I will review the results at least once during every instructional unit and use the information to reteach concepts, adjust student groups, or provide additional practice.

Data Sources Used to Develop Goals

I have developed these goals using the feedback from my internship supervisor, mentor teacher, and field evaluations completed during the MAT program. Observation feedback helped me recognize my growth in lesson planning, classroom management, and student engagement. It also encouraged me to consider how instruction could be adjusted for students who need additional support. I selected this source because observations provide an outside professional perspective on instructional practices that may be difficult to evaluate independently.

The next data source was student achievement data, including written assessments, completed classwork, lab performance rubrics, and student participation. Comparing written work with hands-on performance has shown me that some students can demonstrate a culinary skill but have difficulty explaining the related vocabulary or concepts. Other students understand the content academically but need additional practice applying it during lab. I selected this data source because it provides direct evidence of student learning and helps identify where instructional adjustments are needed.

Self-assessment and reflection also contributed to the development of my goals. Throughout the MAT program, I reflected on my confidence, technology use, classroom management, and ability to meet diverse learning needs. This process helped me recognize that continued professional growth requires an honest review of both successful practices and ongoing challenges.

Alignment of Goals to TAPS Standards

Goal 1 aligns with TAPS Standard 4: Differentiated Instruction. This standard focuses on challenging and supporting students by providing appropriate content and developing learning experiences based on individual needs. This goal also supports TAPS Standard 3: Instructional Strategies. Differentiated lessons require the use of relevant strategies that actively engage students and promote learning.

Goal 2 aligns with TAPS Standard 5: Assessment Strategies and TAPS Standard 6: Assessment Uses. These standards address the teacher’s responsibility to select appropriate assessments, analyze results, provide feedback, and use data to guide instructional decisions. A combination of written, formative, and performance-based assessments will provide a more complete picture of student achievement.

Strategies

Strategy for Goal 1:
I will develop reusable instructional supports for classroom lessons and labs. These resources will include illustrated task cards, vocabulary organizers, recipe checklists, safety reminders, and step-by-step demonstrations. I will use flexible grouping based on student readiness and assign appropriate roles during labs. I will also collaborate with special education teachers and other colleagues to identify accommodations and differentiation practices that support students without lowering expectations.

Strategy for Goal 2:
I will create common performance rubrics for major culinary skills, including knife skills, sanitation, recipe preparation, teamwork, and kitchen organization. I will use brief formative assessments, such as entrance questions, exit tickets, and demonstration checks before students begin a lab. After each unit, I will compare written assessment results with lab performance and student self-assessments. The findings will be used to determine whether students need reteaching, additional modeling, or more practice.

Timeline and Target Dates: One Year Out

August–September 2026: I will review baseline student achievement information, IEP accommodations, prior assessment results, and initial classroom performance. I will select or create differentiation strategies and develop baseline assessments for Goals 1 and 2.

October–December 2026: I will implement at least two differentiated supports per unit. I will begin using common lab-performance rubrics and formative checks. In December, I will review student results and collect feedback about which supports students find most helpful.

January–March 2027: I will revise the instructional supports and assessments based on first-semester results. I will collaborate with colleagues, observe effective practices when possible, and participate in professional learning related to differentiation, assessment, or CTAE instruction.

April–May 2027: I will continue implementing both goals and compare student performance with the baseline data collected at the beginning of the year. I will examine written achievement, lab performance, participation, and student self-assessments for evidence of progress.

June–July 2027: I will complete a final reflection and evaluate my progress toward both goals. By July 2027, I will have a collection of reusable differentiated resources and a balanced assessment system for my Culinary Arts courses. I will use the results to establish new professional goals for the following school year.
